0.4 - BAGONG PILIPINAS Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, west Triangle, Quezon City www.dilq.qov.ph OPINION JUL 23 CHARMAINE OLEA-CAPILI Executive Director 109 s 2024 Philippine Nickel Industry Association Dear Ms. Olea-Capili: This pertains to your letter dated 21 February 2024, in connection with a previou letter dated 28 November 2023. It pertains to a request for this Department's lega view on the legality of regulatory ordinances enacted by various local government units (LGUs) containing provisions imposing taxes/fees for extraction activities conducted by mining companies with Mineral Production Sharing Agreements (MPSA). Your letter claims that these taxes are excessive, duplicative, and inconsistent with the law, rendering them void. You also requested a corresponding Memorandum Circular on this matter. At the outset, allow this Department to discuss that on the duly enacted ordinances by various local government units (LGUs) imposing the assailed taxes, we are constrained to respect the presumptive validity thereof. This is with particular deference and emphasis to the fact that those were enacted pursuant to the revenue- raising and/or regulatory power of local governments. It follows that even with the issuance of the Memorandum Circular you are requesting, the same will not affect the enforceability of the assailed ordinances. Notwithstanding this initial position, and acting on your letter dated 28 November 2023, the Legal and Legislative Liaison Service (LLLS), this Department, forwarded your concern to the Bureau of Local Government Development (BLGD) to explore the possibilities of appropriate measures concerning the request for applicable guidelines. It is coupled with a recommendation that, in the absence of legal basis and applicable policies, the concerned Bureau may consider soliciting comments and/or recommendation of concerned national government agencies. To which, the Bureau responded with an endorsement to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and Department of Finance-Bureau of Local Government Finance (DOF-BLGF). The DENR already responded through the attached letter dated 19 April 2019 on the subject matters that pertains to their mandate. We are yet to receive the response of DOF-BLGF. However, considering your follow-up letter, we deem it prudent to now provide you with the Department's opinion on the following queries you submitted. I) Whether a province can enact an Ordinance imposing one percent (1%) soil depletion tax from gross receipts of all mineral ore extracted, and/or shipped "Matino, Mahusay at Maaasahan" Trunkline No. (02) 8876 3454

2) Whether it is within the power of the province to require for a governor's clearance before the issuance of an Order Transport Permit (OT P)? 3) Whether a province can levy an annual ad valorem tax rate of one percent (1 %) of the assessed value of real property 4) Whether a province can impose a tax on business enjoying a franchise at a rate exceeding fifty percent (50%) of one percent (1%) of the gross annual receipts? 5) Whether a province can impose a fixed amount as to how much tax on sand, gravel and other quarry resources will be collected? 6) Whether a Provincial Governor can issue an industrial sand and gravel permit for an area more than 5 hectares? 7) Whether a Provincial Governor can grant a government gratuitous permit for whatever purpose? On the first query, on whether a province can enact an Ordinance imposing one percent (I %) soil depletion tax from gross receipts of all mineral ore extracted, and/or shipped out, we answer in the affirmative. The assailed soil depletion tax imposed is anchored on LGU's power to create its own sources of revenue authorized under Section 5, Article X, of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, to wit: "(E)ach local government unit shall have the power to create its own sources of revenues and to levy taxes, fees and charges subject to such guidelines and limitations as the Congress may provide, consistent with the basic policy of local autonomy. Consequently, the same is reverberated in Section 129 of R.A. No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991 Interestingly, the purpose of oil depletion tax is not purely revenue-raising but regulatory in nature for environmental protection purposes. As such, it is an environmental protection tax. We put emphasis that this is a case where the LGU uses the term tax in its imposition loosely to include that of regulation purposes. On this we invite attention to the pronouncement of the Supreme Court in Progressive Development Corporation vs. Quezon Cityl. The term "tax" frequently applies to all kinds of exactions of monies which become public funds. It is often loosely used to include levies for revenue as well as levies for regulatory purposes such that license fees are frequently called taxes although license fee is a legal concept distinguishable from tax: the former is imposed in the exercise of police power primarily for purposes of regulation, while the latter is imposed under the taxing power primarily for purposes of raising revenues. As the imposition is not purely of revenue-raising purpose, we do not construe the same as tax specifically on articles or on petroleum products that would fall within the limitations on the taxing power of LGUs in Section 133 (h) of the Local Government Code. 1 G.R. No. L-36081 April 24. 1989 Page 2 of 5

Being the national agency charged with general supervisory power over LGUs with the mandate of assisting them attain self-reliance and full development, it is prudent for this Department to render a liberal construction in favor of local governments as taxing or regulatory entities. If strict scrutiny is to be had, as to whether the same falls within the taxing limitation, we submit that the same is a matter that calls for judicial intervention. As to the 2nd query, whether it is within the power of the province to require for a governor's clearance before the issuance of an Order Transport Permit (OTP), the Mines and Geosciences Bureau of the DENR in its letter dated 19 April 2024 answered in this wise, we quote: "An OTP is a permit that may be granted to a Contractor, accredited dealer, retailer, processor and other permit Holders to transport minerals/mineral products. It is a permit specifying the origin and quantity. It is a permit specifying the origin and quantity of non-processed mineral ores or minerals. It shall be issued by the mines regional director who has jurisdiction over the area where the ores were extracted. The Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB), as the government agency directly in charge in the administration and disposition of mineral lands and mineral resources, shall issue an OTP as long as the applicant satisfies the requirements provided by Republic Act No. 7942 and its Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR). The local government unit (LGU) concerned may impose additional requirements within its jurisdiction." Foregoing considered, we submit that the OTP issued by MGB should necessarily be one of the documentary requirements for the provincial LGUs' issuance of clearances. Yet, we discourage the other way around; that is, to require governor's clearance before issuance of provincial OTP. Requiring private entities to secure OTP from the provincial government in duplication to that secured from MGB may fall within the concept of Bureaucratic Red Tape sought to be avoided. As to the 3rd query, whether a province can levy an annual ad valorem tax rate of one percent (1 of the assessed value of real property, we opine in the affirmative. A province may levy and collect an annual tax on one percent (1%) on the assessed value of the real property which shall be in addition to the basic real property tax, provided the proceeds thereof shall exclusively accrue to the Special Education Fund (SEF). This imposition, although not mandatory, is in accordance with Section 235 of the Local Government Code which provides as follows: Section 235. Additional Levy on Real Property for the Special Education Fund. - A province or city, or a municipality within the Metropolitan Manila Area, may levy and collect an annual tax of one percent (I on the assessed value of real property which shall be in addition to the basic real property tax. The proceeds thereof shall exclusively accrue to the Special Education Fund (SEF). With respect to the 4th query, on whether a province can impose a tax on business enjoying a franchise at a rate exceeding fifty percent (50%) of one percent (I %) of the gross annual receipts, we answer in the negative. Page 3 of 5

Section 137 of the Local Government Code clearly provides that a province may impose a tax on business enjoying franchise, at a rate NOT exceeding fifty percent (50%) of one percent (I %) of the gross annual receipts. To wit: Section 137. Franchise Tax. - Notwithstanding any exemption granted by any law or other special law, the province may impose a tax on businesses enjoying a franchise, at the rate not exceeding fifty percent (50%) of one percent (1%) of the gross annual receipts for the preceding calendar year based on the incoming receipt, or realized, within its territorial jurisdiction. In the case of a newly started business, the tax shall not exceed one- twentieth (1/20) of one percent (1%) of the capital investment. In the succeeding calendar year, regardless of when the business started to operate, the tax shall be based on the gross receipts for the preceding calendar year, or any fraction thereon, as provided herein. Following the aforecited limit provided by the Local Government Code, a province is bereft of authority to impose a tax, on businesses enjoying a franchise, at a rate exceeding fifty percent (50%) of one percent (I %) of the gross annual receipts. On the 5th query, on whether a province can impose a fixed amount as to how much tax on sand, gravel and other quarry resources will be collected, we respond affirmatively subject to the 10% ceiling provided under Section 138 of the Local Government Code, to wit: Section 138. Tax on Sand, Gravel and Other Quarry Resources. - The province may levy and collect not more than ten percent (10%) of fair market value in the locality per cubic meter of ordinary stones, sand, gravel, earth, and other quarry resources, as defined under the National Internal Revenue Code, as amended, extracted from public lands or from the beds of seas, lakes, rivers, streams, creeks, and other public waters within its territorial jurisdiction. The permit to extract sand, gravel and other quarry resources shall be issued exclusively by the provincial governor, pursuant to the ordinance of the sangguniang panlalawigan. The proceeds of the tax on sand, gravel and other quarry resources shall be distributed as follows: (1) Province - Thirty percent (30%); (2) Component City or Municipality where the sand, gravel, and other quarry resources are extracted - Thirty percent (30%); and (3) Barangay where the sand, gravel, and other quarry resources are extracted - Forty percent (40%). Thus, we emphasize that should the province opt to impose a fixed amount of tax on sand, gravel and other quarry resources, the same amount should not exceed the ceiling based on the fair market value per cubic meter. As such, in cases of fixed rate imposition, the ordinance authorizing the same should be regularly updated so as not to violate the limitation provided in the aforesaid provision. Page 4 of 5

On the 6th query, on whether a Provincial Governor can issue an industrial sand and gravel permit for an area more than 5 hectares, we answer in the negative. We quote the answer provided by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau of the DENR: "No, an industrial sand and gravel permit for an area of more than five (5) hectares at any one time is issued by the MGB. Such permit allows a qualified person to undertake the extraction of sand and gravel and other loose or unconsolidated materials which are used in their natural state, without undergoing processing from an area of not more than five (5) hectares."2 In addition, this Department makes it clear that the Provincial Governor may grant a qualified person an industrial sand and gravel permit if the area does not exceed five (5) hectares. On the 7th query, on whether a Provincial Governor can grant a government gratuitous permit for whatever purpose, we likewise adopt the response of the Mines and Geosciences Bureau of the DENR: Section 49 of RA 7942 specifically provides that "any government entity or instrumentality may be granted a gratuitous permit by the provincial governor to extract sand and gravel, quarry of loose unconsolidated materials needed in the construction of building and/or infrastructure for public use or other purposes over an area of not more than two (2) hectares for a period coterminous with said construction". This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to contrary opinion/decision that may be rendered by competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have sufficiently addressed your concerns. Thank you. Respectfully yours, BY AUTHORITY OF THE SECRETARY N OR R. LLAMAS secretary for External, Legal and Legislative Affairs Attachment: Letter dated 19 April 2019 from DENR 2 Section 46, Republic Act No. 7942 Page 5 of 5
